summary:
Pays de la Loire stands under the French national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal procedure, custodial oversight and marriage applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, and the sources document no regional deviation material enough to assess separately. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Custody is the principal exposure. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, who have not had sex-reassignment surgery) are placed in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee recalling inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' alongside threats of violence.

The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, Adeline Hazan, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison. The same feature illustrates her finding with the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in conditions she described as worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority and preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records the persistence of serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees in adult prisons, while noting that none were identified in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres.

That review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. The CGLPL examined roughly forty referrals from trans detainees since 2010 together with ministry and association input, and identified placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches as serious and persistent violations, with structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty; its stated reasons for a new opinion include changed terminology in the gender-recognition law and coverage now extending to intersex and non-binary detainees.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule beyond Article D248: where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

The CGLPL's 2021 opinion drew on inspections spread across several establishments in different parts of France, including Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, and it identified adult prisons as the setting where serious violations persist while mental-health establishments, closed educational centres and juvenile detention centres showed none.

The discrimination reported in services is measured rather than asserted: the Défenseur des droits relies on the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and couples that figure with case files and association testimony in its framework decision for service providers.

Two oversight bodies converge on the same finding from different mandates. Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, names transgender detainees as the group that suffers most in prison, while the CGLPL documents placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches as structural rather than isolated failures.

Legal gender recognition was reformed in 2016, but the CGLPL records no marked improvement in the treatment of trans detainees in the years that followed, which is the reason it gave for issuing a further opinion in 2021 and for extending its terminology and coverage to intersex and non-binary detainees.
localsOnly:
Placement in custody is governed by Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code, which separates men and women into different establishments. Trans people held in France are assigned accordingly to the sex recorded on their identity documents, and each establishment decides on its own whether to use a dedicated unit or isolation, so conditions differ between facilities.

Legal gender recognition has been available under the reform in force since 2016, and marriage between same-sex partners has been available since the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; the first same-sex wedding in France was reported by CNN on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect.

Residents have access to the complaint and inspection machinery that produced these findings: referrals to the CGLPL, which examined roughly forty such referrals from trans detainees since 2010, and the framework decision of the Défenseur des droits, which sets out guidance that service providers are expected to follow.

The isolation of Louna, held in the Tarbes men's prison since mid-October 2024 and in isolation since October, is a matter before the French National Assembly, raised against the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219, and her placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Pays de la Loire-specific detention data appears in the sources: the establishments inspected by the CGLPL are in Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, and the isolation case raised in parliament concerns the Tarbes men's prison. Whether any facility in Pays de la Loire holds trans detainees, and how it places them, is unresolved on this inventory.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented at any named establishment is not sourced here; the opinion itself records no marked improvement since 2010, but no post-2021 compliance assessment is available in this material.

The scale of identity-document friction at French entry points rests on a single first-person account of 7 March 2017. No aggregate or official statistics on border checks of trans travellers' documents are available in this inventory, and any regional variation in enforcement at airports serving Pays de la Loire is not sourced.

It is not established from these sources how many of the roughly forty transgender detainees reviewed by the CGLPL were placed in facilities within Pays de la Loire, or whether outcomes for trans residents of the region differ from the national picture.
